Low signal strength; increase AP transmit power
Band steering failure; disable the 5 GHz radios on the APs
Hidden SSID; advertise the SSID in beacons

explanation: Channels 3 and 9 overlap with 1 and 6 and with 6 and 11, causing adjacent-channel interference and retries; using only 1, 6 and 11 removes the overlap. Raising power makes overlap worse. Disabling 5 GHz pushes more clients into the congested band. SSID visibility does not affect interference.

prompt: A dense lecture hall with 12 APs uses 80 MHz channels in the 5 GHz band. Survey data shows several APs sharing the same channel, high channel utilisation and poor per-client throughput, even though signal strength is strong. What should be changed?

options.text: Increase the channel width to 160 MHz
Move all of the clients to 2.4 GHz
Turn off half of the APs in the hall
Reduce the channel width to 20 or 40 MHz

explanation: Wide channels reduce the number of separate channels, so in a dense area APs end up sharing them and contending for airtime; narrower channels allow better channel reuse and less co-channel interference. 160 MHz makes the shortage worse. Turning off APs reduces capacity in a dense hall. 2.4 GHz has even fewer channels and more interference.

prompt: A user walks from one wing to another and keeps an RSSI of -80 dBm to the original AP even when standing beside another AP at -45 dBm. Throughput is poor until Wi-Fi is turned off and on. What is this issue called, and what helps fix it?

options.text: A band steering issue; disable the 5 GHz band on the APs
Channel overlap; change the APs' channels
A sticky client; enable 802.11k/v and a minimum RSSI
An evil twin AP; enable WIPS containment

explanation: A client that stays associated with a distant AP when a much better one is nearby is a sticky client; 802.11k neighbour reports, 802.11v BSS transition requests and minimum RSSI thresholds encourage it to roam. Disabling 5 GHz does not make clients roam better. Channel overlap causes interference, not a failure to roam. An evil twin is an impostor AP, and the client here is on a legitimate AP.

prompt: After aggressive band steering was enabled on a dual-band SSID, handheld scanners that support only 2.4 GHz take a long time to connect or fail to connect, while laptops work well on 5 GHz. What is the best fix?

options.text: Disable the 2.4 GHz radios on all of the APs
Relax band steering, or give the scanners their own SSID
Enable 802.11r fast roaming on the dual-band corporate SSID
Increase 5 GHz transmit power across the floor

explanation: Aggressive band steering ignores or delays 2.4 GHz probe responses to push clients to 5 GHz, which hurts clients that cannot use 5 GHz; relaxing the steering or using a separate SSID fixes it. Disabling 2.4 GHz would disconnect the scanners entirely. More 5 GHz power does not help 2.4 GHz-only devices. 802.11r speeds up roaming but does not affect band steering.

prompt: After a conference room was renovated with metal-coated low-emissivity glass walls, signal in the room fell from -60 dBm to -82 dBm and users disconnect frequently. Channel and interference readings are unchanged. What is the best solution?

options.text: Raise the distant APs' transmit power to maximum
Add an AP inside the conference room
Switch the room's clients to 2.4 GHz only
Enable MAC filtering in the room

explanation: Metal-coated glass heavily attenuates RF, so the room now has signal loss from outside APs; an AP inside the room gives strong signal again. Maximum power on distant APs adds interference elsewhere and does not fix the client's weak return path. 2.4 GHz penetrates somewhat better but gives lower capacity and does not solve the problem well. MAC filtering does not affect signal strength.

prompt: After 802.11r Fast BSS Transition was enabled on the corporate SSID in FT-only mode, a group of older barcode printers can no longer join the WLAN, though laptops and phones roam well. What is the issue, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The printers' DHCP scope is full; enlarge the printer scope
The printers' signal is too weak; add more APs
No 802.11r support; use FT mixed mode or a separate SSID
Channel width is too narrow; increase it to 80 MHz

explanation: Some older clients do not understand the FT information in beacons and probe responses and cannot associate to an FT-only SSID; mixed mode or a separate SSID restores compatibility. Signal strength would not change because of the FT setting. A full scope would let the printers associate but not get addresses. Channel width does not affect whether the FT capability is supported.

prompt: A hospital is deploying Wi-Fi voice badges. In one ward, a survey shows RSSI of -70 dBm with a noise floor of -88 dBm. Calls are choppy, and the badge vendor requires at least -67 dBm and an SNR of 25 dB. What is the issue?

options.text: The noise floor is too low for the badges to work
The SNR of 158 dB is overloading the badge receivers
SNR of 18 dB and weak signal; add or relocate APs
The badges are sticky clients that do not roam

explanation: SNR is the signal minus the noise floor, -70 minus -88, which is 18 dB, below the 25 dB requirement, and -70 dBm is also below the -67 dBm minimum, so voice coverage is too weak. Adding the absolute values to get 158 dB is wrong. A lower noise floor is better, not worse. There is no evidence of failure to roam, only weak signal.

prompt: Clients across one building are repeatedly disconnected from the WLAN several times a minute. The WIPS reports a high rate of deauthentication frames that appear to come from the corporate APs' BSSIDs, but the APs' own logs show they sent none. What is happening, and which control mitigates it?

options.text: Normal roaming behaviour; no action is needed
Spoofed deauthentication attack; enable 802.11w PMF
An overloaded DHCP server; add a second server
Channel overlap; change the channels on the APs

explanation: Deauth frames that claim to come from the APs but were not sent by them are spoofed, and an attacker uses them to force clients off the network; 802.11w Protected Management Frames lets clients reject unauthenticated deauth frames. Roaming does not produce floods of spoofed deauths. Channel overlap causes retries, not deauthentication. DHCP problems cause addressing failures, not repeated disassociation.

prompt: A new application VM cannot be reached on TCP 443 from the load balancer, while identical VMs in the same subnet work. The working VMs belong to security group 'sg-web', and the new VM belongs only to 'sg-default', which allows no inbound traffic. What is the fix?

options.text: Add a route to the load balancer subnet
Restart the load balancer
Disable the host firewall on the load balancer
Attach the new VM to the 'sg-web' security group

explanation: The new VM was given the wrong security group, so the inbound rule allowing 443 from the load balancer does not apply to it; attaching sg-web fixes it. Routing is the same for VMs in the same subnet. Restarting the load balancer does not change the VM's security group. The load balancer's host firewall is not involved, since other VMs work.

prompt: A web tier in one security group cannot query a new PostgreSQL cluster in another security group. The database group allows inbound TCP 5432 from the web group. The web group's outbound rules allow only TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0. What is the cause?

options.text: PostgreSQL must be moved to listen on TCP 443
The database group needs an outbound rule for TCP 5432
Security groups are stateless, so return traffic must be allowed
The web group lacks an outbound rule for TCP 5432

explanation: The web servers start the connection, so their security group needs an outbound rule allowing TCP 5432 to the database group; the outbound rules allow only 443. Because security groups are stateful, the database group needs no outbound rule for return traffic. Stateless filtering applies to network ACLs, not security groups. Changing PostgreSQL's port is unnecessary.

prompt:
An audit reveals that RDP from the internet reaches a jump server despite a rule intended to allow RDP only from the corporate VPN range. The firewall policy is:

1  Allow  Any            -> 10.1.0.0/16  Any
2  Allow  10.99.0.0/16   -> 10.1.5.10    TCP 3389
3  Deny   Any            -> Any          Any

What is the problem?

options.text: Rule 2 has the wrong destination address for the server
The deny rule 3 should be moved to the top of the policy
Rule 1 is overly permissive and matches before rule 2
The firewall cannot filter RDP because it is encrypted

explanation: Rules are processed top-down, and rule 1 allows any source to any port in 10.1.0.0/16, which includes the jump server, so rule 2's restriction never takes effect; rule 1 must be removed or narrowed. Rule 2's destination is correct. Moving the deny-all to the top would block everything. RDP is ordinary TCP 3389 traffic that any firewall can filter.

prompt: Since this morning, users cannot open a newly adopted SaaS project tool. The browser shows the secure web gateway's block page with the category 'Newly Registered Domains', although the vendor's domain was registered two years ago and the company has approved the tool. What should be done?

options.text: Disable URL filtering for all users until the vendor responds
Also block the Newly Registered Domains category on every other edge firewall
Tell users to reach the tool from their personal mobile phones
Override the category for the vendor's domains and request recategorisation

explanation: The SaaS domain has been miscategorised, so an allow-list entry or override restores access at once, and a recategorisation request fixes it at the source. Disabling URL filtering removes protection for everyone. Using mobile phones bypasses security controls. Blocking the category elsewhere does not unblock the approved tool.

prompt: A partner reports that its users suddenly receive HTTP 403 errors from the company's CDN-fronted portal. CDN logs show the requests as blocked by a geo-restriction rule, with the client country listed as 'NL', although the partner is in Germany, which is allowed. The partner recently moved to a cloud-hosted secure web gateway. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The partner's client TLS certificate has expired
The partner's new SWG egress IPs geolocate to the Netherlands
The portal's public DNS record points to the wrong CDN
The CDN is under a DDoS attack and blocking some sources

explanation: Geo-restriction uses the source IP's geolocation, and the partner's new SWG sends traffic from egress IPs registered in the Netherlands; allowing that country or the SWG's known egress ranges resolves it. Clients do not normally present certificates to a public portal, and an expiry would not cause a geo-block. A DNS error would stop users reaching the CDN at all. A DDoS attack does not explain a country-based block of one partner.

prompt:
An ACL was applied to a router's LAN interface to allow only web traffic from the user subnet 10.10.0.0/24 to the internet:

access-list WEB-OUT permit tcp 10.10.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
interface Gi0/1 (LAN side)
 ip access-group WEB-OUT out

Users can no longer reach anything, including HTTPS. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: HTTPS must be permitted on TCP 80 as well as 443
The ACL also needs a permit entry for UDP 443 so QUIC can pass
The wildcard mask should be 255.255.255.0 instead
The ACL is applied in the wrong direction on the LAN interface

explanation: Traffic from users enters the LAN interface inbound; applied outbound, the ACL checks traffic going toward users, whose source is the internet, so nothing matches the 10.10.0.0/24 source and the implicit deny drops it, including HTTPS replies. A UDP 443 entry would help only QUIC, not explain the total outage. 0.0.0.255 is the correct wildcard for a /24. HTTPS uses TCP 443.

prompt:
A public web server becomes unresponsive. On the server:

$ ss -tan state syn-recv | wc -l
65012
$ ss -tan state established | wc -l
214

Packet captures show SYNs from thousands of random source IPs with no following ACKs. What is happening, and which control mitigates it on the host?

options.text: A SYN flood; enable SYN cookies and upstream protection
Slow application responses; add more worker threads
Asymmetric routing; fix the return routes for the server
Outbound port exhaustion; widen the ephemeral port range

explanation: Tens of thousands of half-open connections in SYN-RECV from random sources that never complete the handshake is a SYN flood; SYN cookies let the host handle connections without keeping state for each half-open one, and upstream protection absorbs volume. Ephemeral port exhaustion affects outbound connections, not inbound SYN-RECV. More worker threads do not help with handshakes that never complete. Asymmetric routing would not produce SYNs from thousands of random sources.

prompt: After the security team rotated the RADIUS shared secret on the server, all 802.1X authentications on one building's switches fail, while other buildings work. The server logs show messages about invalid Message-Authenticator attributes from those switches' IPs. What is the cause?

options.text: The users' passwords expired when the secret was rotated
The RADIUS server's certificate has been revoked
The building's switches still use the old shared secret
The building's switches are in the wrong VLAN

explanation: The Message-Authenticator is computed with the shared secret, so invalid values from one set of switches show that they still have the old secret; updating it on those switches fixes the problem. Expired passwords would affect users in every building and produce Access-Rejects, not authenticator errors. A revoked server certificate would affect EAP-TLS clients everywhere. A VLAN problem would stop packets reaching the server, not produce authenticator errors.

prompt: A network engineer can log in through SSO to the cloud network management console but gets 'access denied' when trying to edit firewall policies. Colleagues with the same job title can edit them. The SAML assertion for the engineer contains no 'netadmins' group claim, while the colleagues' assertions do. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The engineer is missing from the group mapped to the editor role
The SAML signing certificate used by the management console has expired
The engineer's MFA token has expired since sign-in
The console is under a DDoS attack affecting changes

explanation: Authentication works but authorisation fails, and the assertion has no group claim, so the engineer is missing from the group that maps to the editing role; adding the membership fixes it. An expired MFA token would stop sign-in. An expired signing certificate would break SSO for everyone. A DDoS would affect all users, not just authorisation for one.

prompt:
An internal tool fails to call a partner API, and curl shows:

$ curl -v https://api.partner.example
* Server certificate:
*  subject: CN=www.partner.example
*  subjectAltName does not match api.partner.example
* SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'api.partner.example'

What is the issue?

options.text: The partner's server certificate has expired
The certificate's SAN does not include api.partner.example
The client does not trust the partner's issuing CA
The client library does not support TLS 1.3 handshakes

explanation: curl reports that no SAN entry matches the requested host name, so the server is presenting the wrong certificate; it needs a certificate that covers api.partner.example, or the right SNI-based certificate selection. An expired certificate would produce an expiry error. An untrusted CA would show a chain verification error. A TLS version problem would fail during the handshake with a protocol error.

prompt:
A VPN client fails to connect, reporting that the gateway's certificate is invalid. The engineer checks the certificate's status:

$ openssl ocsp -issuer issuing-ca.pem -cert vpn-gw.pem -url http://ocsp.example.com -resp_text
...
vpn-gw.pem: revoked
    This Update: Nov 23 08:00:00 2026 GMT
    Reason: keyCompromise
    Revocation Time: Nov 22 19:14:03 2026 GMT

What should be done?

options.text: Issue a new key pair and certificate and investigate the compromise
Extend the validity period of the existing gateway certificate
Install the issuing root CA certificate on all clients
Disable certificate revocation checking on the VPN clients

explanation: The OCSP responder reports the certificate as revoked for key compromise, so the gateway needs a new key pair and certificate, and the compromise must be investigated. Disabling revocation checks would accept a compromised key. The validity period is irrelevant once a certificate is revoked. The trust chain is not the problem; the certificate itself is revoked.

prompt:
After a load balancer was hardened to accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, a legacy reporting client can no longer connect. A test from the client host shows:

$ openssl s_client -connect reports.example.com:443 -tls1_1
... alert protocol version ...
$ openssl s_client -connect reports.example.com:443 -tls1_2
... Protocol: TLSv1.2, Cipher: ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256, Verify return code: 0 (ok)

The legacy client's library supports only TLS 1.0 and 1.1. What is the issue, and what is the best resolution?

options.text: The server certificate has expired; renew it
The client does not trust the CA; add it to the trust store
TLS version mismatch; upgrade the client's TLS library
The server uses the wrong cipher suite; enable RC4

explanation: The server rejects TLS 1.1 with a protocol version alert and accepts TLS 1.2, so the problem is a version mismatch; the secure fix is to update the client so it supports TLS 1.2 or later, since TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996. Verification returns OK, so neither expiry nor trust is the issue. RC4 is prohibited and would not fix a protocol version mismatch.

prompt: A new branch firewall's WAN interface received 100.72.14.9/10 from the ISP by DHCP. Outbound internet access works, but a port forward for TCP 443 to an internal server is unreachable from the internet. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The /10 mask is too large for the firewall to apply destination NAT
The address is an RFC 1918 private address, which the firewall cannot use for port forwarding rules
The address is in RFC 6598 shared space for carrier-grade NAT
The address is an IPv6-mapped IPv4 address that needs NAT64 for inbound traffic

explanation: 100.64.0.0/10 is the shared address space defined in RFC 6598 for carrier-grade NAT, so inbound connections hit the ISP's NAT and never reach the firewall; the branch needs a public address from the ISP. It is not an RFC 1918 range, which covers 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. The prefix length does not stop destination NAT on the firewall. It is a plain IPv4 address, not an IPv6-mapped one, so NAT64 is irrelevant.

prompt: A company received a /48 IPv6 allocation for a campus. Each user VLAN must support SLAAC so clients can configure their own addresses. Which prefix length should be assigned to each VLAN?

options.text: /56, to leave room for growth inside each VLAN
/127, as used on point-to-point links
/112, to conserve address space as in IPv4

explanation: SLAAC builds a 64-bit interface identifier, so each LAN segment needs a /64, and a /48 provides 65,536 of them. A /56 is a common allocation for a whole site or customer, not a single VLAN, and SLAAC will not work with it on one link. A /112 breaks SLAAC and conserving addresses this way is unnecessary in IPv6. A /127 is recommended for point-to-point router links (RFC 6164), not for client VLANs.

prompt: A web application authenticates users by performing an LDAP simple bind against the directory on TCP 389. A packet capture shows user passwords in clear text. Which change protects the credentials while keeping directory authentication?

options.text: Switch the application to RADIUS with PAP against the same directory
Move the binds to TACACS+ on TCP 49 for full payload encryption
Use LDAP over TLS, either LDAPS on TCP 636 or StartTLS on TCP 389
Keep simple binds on TCP 389 but require longer user passwords

explanation: LDAPS (TCP 636) or StartTLS on 389 wraps the LDAP session in TLS, so the bind credentials are encrypted while the application keeps using the directory. RADIUS with PAP hides the password only with a shared-secret obfuscation and is not a directory protocol for applications. TACACS+ is designed for device administration AAA, not application directory lookups. Longer passwords are still sent in clear text.

prompt: A new VXLAN fabric carries VM traffic whose MTU is 1500 bytes. Small packets cross the fabric, but large transfers between hosts on different leaves stall. The underlay interfaces are all at the default MTU of 1500. What should be changed?

options.text: Lower the VM MTU to 1400 and leave the underlay unchanged so that no fabric change is needed
Replace VXLAN with 802.1Q trunks between all leaves
Raise the underlay MTU to at least 1550 bytes, commonly to 9000 or more
Enable spanning tree on the underlay links

explanation: VXLAN over IPv4 adds about 50 bytes (outer Ethernet, IP, UDP and VXLAN headers), so a full 1500-byte inner frame needs an underlay MTU of at least 1550; jumbo frames are the usual design. Lowering every VM's MTU works around the problem but is error-prone and is not the standard design. Replacing VXLAN with trunks loses the routed underlay. Spanning tree is not used on a routed underlay and has nothing to do with MTU.

prompt: An architect is classifying traffic flows for a three-tier web application in a cloud VPC. Which two flows are east/west traffic? (Choose two.)

options.text: Internet users connecting to the public load balancer
The web tier calling the application tier's API
The application tier querying the database tier
Application servers downloading OS patches from the internet
Remote employees connecting through the VPN to the web tier

explanation: East/west traffic moves between workloads inside the environment, such as web to application and application to database. Internet users reaching the load balancer, servers downloading patches from the internet, and VPN users entering the network all cross the boundary of the environment, which makes them north/south flows.

prompt: Twelve branches connect over IPsec to the corporate network. Branches rarely talk to each other, but each must stay connected if one hub data centre fails. Which topology gives this resilience at the lowest tunnel count?

options.text: A full mesh of tunnels between all twelve branches and both hubs
A dual-hub hub-and-spoke design with each branch tunnelled to both hubs
Point-to-point tunnels between each pair of neighbouring branches in a ring
A single hub-and-spoke design with every branch tunnelled to the primary hub

explanation: With two hubs, each branch needs only two tunnels (24 in total) and survives the loss of either hub. A full mesh among 14 sites needs 91 tunnels for branch-to-branch traffic that hardly exists. A single hub leaves every branch cut off if that hub fails. A ring makes traffic transit other branches and gives poor resilience to a hub failure.

prompt: A construction company sets up temporary site offices that last three to six months. Each needs internet and VPN access within a day of arrival, and wired circuits take weeks to install. Which connectivity choice fits best?

options.text: A 5G/LTE router with dual-carrier SIMs running the VPN
A dark fiber lease from the nearest exchange, lit with the company's optics
A metro Ethernet circuit ordered at each new site
An MPLS L3VPN circuit added to the existing WAN contract

explanation: Cellular routers can be deployed the same day, and SIMs from two carriers give some redundancy for the VPN. Dark fiber, metro Ethernet and MPLS circuits all need physical installation that takes weeks, and their contract terms are usually far longer than a few months.

prompt: A company is migrating a web portal in stages. During the migration, one public hostname must send /legacy/* requests to servers still on premises, reachable over the private cloud circuit, and /api/* to new containers in the cloud, with TLS terminated in one place. Which solution fits?

options.text: A DNS round robin record listing both the on-premises and the cloud addresses
A layer 4 load balancer in the cloud with the on-premises servers added to its pool
Two separate hostnames, one published by each environment's firewall
A layer 7 application gateway with path rules and hybrid backend pools

explanation: An application gateway terminates TLS once, routes by URL path, and can use private on-premises IP addresses reached over the circuit as backend targets alongside cloud containers. DNS round robin cannot split traffic by path. A layer 4 load balancer sees only IPs and ports, so it cannot route by path. Two hostnames break the requirement for one public hostname.

prompt: Logs show constant brute-force attempts against TCP 3389 on a server that offers RDP to remote support staff from the internet. Staff still need RDP sessions to internal servers without a full VPN. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a remote desktop gateway over TLS 443 with MFA; close 3389
Keep RDP open to the internet but enable account lockout after five failures
Allow RDP only from the countries where support staff live
Move RDP to TCP 3390 on the same server to avoid automated scanners

explanation: A remote desktop gateway wraps RDP in TLS, enforces MFA before any session reaches an internal server, and lets TCP 3389 be closed to the internet. Moving to another port is found quickly by scanners. Lockout still leaves RDP exposed and lets attackers lock out real users. Geolocation restrictions are easily bypassed and leave the service exposed.

prompt: A report-rendering service receives requests whose CPU cost varies from milliseconds to several minutes. Connection counts are similar across servers, yet some servers sit at 100% CPU while others are idle. Each server publishes its current CPU and queue depth to the load balancer. Which method should be configured?

options.text: Least connections
Weighted round robin with static weights
Round robin with session persistence
Load-based balancing on reported CPU and queue

explanation: Load-based balancing uses the servers' reported resource use, so new work goes to servers with spare CPU, which suits requests of very different cost. Least connections counts connections, which are similar here and do not reflect CPU load. Round robin with persistence ignores load and pins users to busy servers. Static weights reflect fixed capacity, not current load.

prompt: During an outage, an application returned HTTP 500 errors for every request, but the load balancer kept sending traffic to all servers because each still accepted TCP connections on port 443. What change best prevents this?

options.text: Shorten the TCP health-check interval to 2 seconds so failures are found sooner
Use an HTTP health check on a deep endpoint; fail on non-200
Switch from round robin to least connections
Add more servers to the pool

explanation: A TCP check only proves that the port accepts connections; an HTTP check against a meaningful health endpoint detects application failures and removes broken servers from rotation. A shorter TCP interval still passes every check. Changing the balancing method does not detect failures. More servers would also fail the same way.

prompt: An application needs 6 instances at peak. It runs in an autoscaling group spread evenly across three availability zones and must still have 6 instances at peak if one whole zone fails. What is the minimum number of instances to run at peak?
explanation: If one of three zones fails, the remaining two zones must hold 6 instances, so each zone needs 3, which is 9 in total. Running 6 leaves only 4 after a zone failure. With 8 spread evenly, a zone loss can leave only 5. Running 12 works but is more than the minimum.

prompt: Each rack has dual-corded servers fed from an A-side PDU and a B-side PDU on separate circuits. Monitoring shows each side carrying 70% of its circuit's rated capacity. What is the risk?

options.text: A and B circuits must be on the same breaker for the power supplies to share load
Dual-corded servers draw full power from both sides at once, so the rack uses double its rated power
A failed side would leave the other at about 140%, so keep each below 50%
The PDUs should be swapped for basic power strips to reduce losses

explanation: Dual-corded loads share power across both feeds, so when one feed fails the other carries the whole load; at 70% per side that is about 140%, which overloads it, so each side must stay under 50%. Servers split their draw rather than taking full power from both sides. Putting both feeds on one breaker defeats the redundancy. Power strips offer no monitoring and do not fix the overload.

prompt: A company is moving network appliances from a North American site running 120 V to a European data centre that supplies 230 V. Which check matters most before the equipment is powered on?

options.text: That the rack PDUs are switched rather than metered models
That the BTU rating of each appliance is printed on its rating label
That the UPS runtime is the same as at the original site
That the PSUs accept 230 V input, such as 100–240 V auto-ranging

explanation: A power supply that accepts only about 120 V can be damaged on 230 V, so the input range must be confirmed (most modern units auto-range from 100 to 240 V) along with the right cords. Switched or metered PDUs give control and monitoring, not voltage compatibility. UPS runtime matters for outages, not for safe power-on. BTU ratings help with cooling planning, not voltage safety.

prompt: Staff complain that the new fingerprint readers at the data hall often reject them, causing queues at shift change. The security manager plans to lower the matching threshold. What trade-off should the architect point out?

options.text: Lowering the threshold raises both the false rejection and false acceptance rates
It cuts false rejections but raises the false acceptance rate
Lowering the threshold has no effect on accuracy, only on read speed
Lowering the threshold makes the readers fail closed during power cuts

explanation: Biometric systems trade false rejection against false acceptance: a looser match accepts more real users but also more impostors, so the threshold must balance convenience with security (the crossover error rate marks where the two are equal). The two rates move in opposite directions, not together. The threshold directly changes accuracy, not just speed. Failure behaviour during power loss is a separate lock design choice.

prompt: A company is moving to a cloud meeting service that uses SIP, but it has 40 conference room systems that support only H.323 and must stay in service for two more years. What should the architect provide?

options.text: An H.323-to-SIP gateway or the provider's H.323 interop service
An RTSP server to re-stream the room video into the cloud meeting service
WebRTC browsers installed on each room system
Upgrade the room systems' PoE to PoE+ so they can run SIP

explanation: H.323 and SIP are different signalling protocols, so a gateway or the provider's interop service is needed to translate between them while the old room systems stay in use. PoE class does not change the protocols a device supports. RTSP is a streaming control protocol and does not provide two-way calls. Room appliances usually cannot run arbitrary browsers, and that would not make the existing H.323 systems interoperate.

prompt: A carrier delivers a new internet circuit to the MDF with a handoff on single-mode fiber, terminated on the carrier's network termination device (CPE). The company's firewall has only copper RJ45 ports and one empty SFP slot. What should be ordered to connect the firewall?

options.text: A 1000BASE-SX SFP with multimode patch cords to the CPE
A single-mode 1000BASE-LX SFP or single-mode media converter
A Cat6A patch cable from the CPE fiber port to the firewall's copper port
A 10GBASE-SR SFP+ module

explanation: The handoff is single-mode fiber, so the firewall needs a single-mode optic such as 1000BASE-LX in its SFP slot, or a single-mode media converter to copper. 1000BASE-SX uses multimode fiber and wavelengths that do not match the carrier's optics. A copper cable cannot plug into a fiber port. 10GBASE-SR is a multimode 10 Gbps optic that does not match the circuit or most SFP slots.

prompt: In a busy IDF, technicians often unplug the wrong patch cord, and some switches overheat because cables hang in front of their exhaust vents. Which improvement addresses both problems?

options.text: Add a second cooling unit to the IDF and keep the current cabling as it is
Replace all copper patch cords with fiber to reduce bulk
Move the IDF switches to the MDF
Cable managers, right-length cords clear of vents, TIA-606 labels

explanation: Proper cable management with cable managers, right-length cords and routing clear of vents restores airflow, and consistent labelling of both ends stops technicians unplugging the wrong cord. Fiber does not fix labelling or routing. Moving switches to the MDF breaks horizontal cable distance limits. Extra cooling does not clear the blocked vents and does nothing for the mislabelled cords.

prompt: A stadium is replacing older 802.11ac APs. The venue has tens of thousands of clients sending small, bursty packets, and performance collapses during events. Which standard feature most directly improves efficiency for many simultaneous small transmissions?

options.text: 802.11ac Wave 2 downlink MU-MIMO only
Wider 160 MHz channels on every AP to increase per-client throughput
Hidden SSIDs to reduce probe traffic
802.11ax OFDMA serving several clients per transmission

explanation: OFDMA in 802.11ax divides a channel into resource units so several clients can be served at once, cutting overhead for many small packets; BSS colouring further reduces co-channel contention. Downlink MU-MIMO in 802.11ac helps a few capable clients with large transfers, not thousands of small bursts. Wide channels reduce the number of channels available and worsen contention in dense areas. Hidden SSIDs increase probing rather than reducing it.

prompt: A five-storey office uses ceiling-mounted omni-directional APs. Surveys show strong signal from APs on the floors above and below, causing co-channel interference. Which placement approach reduces this?

options.text: Mount every AP directly above the AP on the floor below, on the same channel
Mount APs on the walls facing upward
Increase transmit power on all APs so that clients prefer their own floor
Stagger APs between floors and plan channels in 3D

explanation: RF passes through floors, so staggering APs and planning channels across floors as well as across each floor keeps vertically adjacent APs on different channels. Stacking APs on the same channel maximises interference between floors. Raising power increases bleed to other floors. Pointing antennas upward sends more energy into the floor above.

prompt: The help desk receives dozens of tickets a week for the same VPN client error after OS updates. Engineers fixed it each time by clearing a cached profile. The help desk wants to resolve these tickets itself. Which artifact should be created?

options.text: A knowledge base article with symptom, cause and fix
A low-level design for the VPN service
A new statement of work for the VPN vendor to support the help desk
A work breakdown structure for the VPN platform

explanation: A knowledge base article captures a known problem, its symptoms, cause and fix so first-line staff can resolve repeat issues. A low-level design describes how the service is built, not how to fix a client error. An SOW defines contracted project work. A WBS breaks down project deliverables.

prompt: NOC engineers troubleshooting routing need a diagram that shows each site's VRFs, subnets, routing protocol areas and BGP peerings, without rack positions or cable details. Which diagram should be maintained?

options.text: A physical diagram with rack elevations and patch-panel port maps
A logical diagram of Layer 3 domains and adjacencies
A data flow diagram for each business application
A floor plan showing cable routes and IDF locations

explanation: A logical diagram shows how the network works at Layer 2 and 3, with subnets, VRFs, areas and peerings, which is what routing troubleshooting needs. A physical diagram shows hardware placement and cabling. A data flow diagram follows application data, not routing domains. A floor plan shows physical cable routes.

prompt: Midway through a contracted data centre migration, the company asks the contractor to also replace the wireless controllers, which the statement of work does not mention. What is the correct way to handle this?

options.text: The contractor should do the work, because the SOW covers all network tasks
The company's engineers should add it to the existing WBS without telling the contractor
Raise a change request amending the SOW's scope, cost and schedule
Record it as a risk in the risk register and proceed

explanation: Work outside the agreed SOW is a scope change and needs a formal change request or SOW amendment covering scope, cost and timeline. The SOW defines exactly what is in scope, so it does not cover unlisted tasks. Changing an internal WBS does not alter the contract. A risk register entry does not authorise or fund new work.

prompt: An IDS alert on traffic to a VPN appliance's web service shows a request containing several hundred bytes of 0x90 followed by binary shellcode in an HTTP header field. Which attack does this indicate, and what is the primary mitigation?

options.text: A SQL injection attempt; add parameterised queries to the appliance
A buffer overflow with a NOP sled; patch, with IPS meanwhile
A credential stuffing attempt; enforce MFA on the VPN
An on-path attack; enable HSTS on the appliance

explanation: A long run of 0x90 (NOP) bytes followed by shellcode is a classic NOP sled used in buffer overflow exploits, which overwrite memory to run attacker code; the fix is patching, with IPS signatures as a stopgap. SQL injection uses query syntax, not binary shellcode. Credential stuffing uses valid username and password pairs. An on-path attack intercepts traffic rather than sending exploit payloads.

prompt: Cloud audit logs show that a developer's identity, which has a limited role, called the IAM API to attach an administrator policy to itself and then created new access keys. Which threat is this, and which control best prevents it?

options.text: Data exfiltration; enable DLP on the storage service
IP spoofing; enable uRPF on the VPC edge
Privilege escalation; remove its IAM-modify rights and alert
A zero-day exploit; wait for the cloud provider's patch

explanation: An identity granting itself higher permissions is privilege escalation; it was possible because the role could modify IAM policies, so least privilege must remove that right, with alerts on IAM changes. Data exfiltration may follow but is not what the log shows. IP spoofing is a network-layer attack. Misused permissions are a configuration problem, not a provider zero-day.

prompt: The help desk received a call from someone claiming to be the CFO, travelling and urgent, demanding an immediate MFA reset and a new temporary password. The caller ID matched the CFO's mobile number. What should the help desk procedure require?

options.text: Verify identity through an independent channel, such as a directory callback
Email the temporary password to the CFO's address so it reaches the right person
Ask the caller to confirm their employee number before resetting
Reset the MFA because the caller ID matches

explanation: This is a social engineering (vishing) pattern using urgency and authority, and caller ID can be spoofed, so identity must be verified through a channel the caller does not control. Trusting caller ID is unsafe. Emailing a password to an account the attacker may already control is unsafe. Employee numbers are often easy to find and are weak proof of identity.

prompt: A review of a core router's 900-line ACL finds many entries referencing subnets decommissioned years ago, several 'permit ip any host' lines added for long-finished projects, and no comments or owners. Which vulnerability does this describe, and what is the best mitigation?

options.text: A zero-day vulnerability; apply the latest router firmware
Legacy ACLs; review, remove stale entries, assign owners
An IP spoofing vulnerability; enable uRPF on all interfaces
An insecure protocol; disable SSH on the router

explanation: Stale and overly broad ACL entries are a legacy ACL vulnerability, since forgotten permits keep access open; configuration reviews with owners and periodic recertification fix and prevent it. Firmware updates do not change ACL content. uRPF addresses spoofed sources, not stale permits. SSH is a secure management protocol and is unrelated to ACL hygiene.

prompt: The SOC wants its network IDS to detect previously unseen attacks for which no signature exists, such as a host suddenly scanning hundreds of internal ports at 03:00. It accepts more tuning effort in return. Which detection approach should be added?

options.text: A web application firewall in front of all internal servers
More frequent updates of the signature database
Anomaly-based detection from a behavioural baseline
Static firewall block lists of known-bad IPs

explanation: Anomaly-based detection learns normal traffic patterns and alerts on deviations, so it can catch new attacks without signatures, at the cost of more false positives and tuning. Signature updates only cover attacks that are already known. A WAF protects web applications, not internal port scanning. Block lists contain only known-bad sources.

prompt: Battery-powered IoT gateways with limited CPU must use TLS with certificate authentication. The security standard requires strength comparable to RSA 3072 while keeping handshake cost and certificate size small. Which certificate key type should be chosen?

options.text: ECDSA P-256
RSA 4096
DSA 1024
RSA 2048 with SHA-1 signatures

explanation: ECDSA with the P-256 curve gives security roughly equal to RSA 3072 with much smaller keys and cheaper signing, which suits constrained devices. RSA 4096 is stronger but expensive for small CPUs and makes certificates larger. DSA 1024 is too weak and is deprecated. RSA 2048 is below the required strength, and SHA-1 signatures are no longer accepted.

prompt: Dozens of internal microservices call each other over the network. The security team requires every connection to be encrypted and both client and server to prove their identity without shared passwords or API keys. Which protocol approach meets this?

options.text: Server-only TLS with API keys in request headers
IPsec transport mode with one pre-shared key for all hosts
HTTP basic authentication over TLS
Mutual TLS, using certificates from an internal CA for every service

explanation: Mutual TLS makes both sides present certificates during the handshake, giving encryption and two-way authentication without shared secrets. Server-only TLS authenticates just the server, and API keys are shared secrets. One PSK for every host is a shared secret that cannot identify individual services. Basic authentication sends a password with each request.

prompt: Web servers in an autoscaling group get new private IPs every time they scale, and the database security rule that allows them by listing IP addresses keeps going out of date. How should the inbound rule on the database be written?

options.text: Allow the database port from the whole VPC CIDR
Update the IP list with a script every hour
Use the web tier's security group or tag as the source
Allow the database port from 0.0.0.0/0 and rely on database passwords

explanation: Referencing the web tier's security group or tag as the source means any instance in that group is allowed, whatever its IP, so the rule stays correct as instances scale. The whole VPC CIDR admits every workload, breaking least privilege. An hourly script leaves gaps and is fragile. Opening to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the database broadly.

prompt:
An inline IPS has this custom rule, but exploit attempts against the backup script still reach the server, though alerts are logged:

alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET 8080 (msg:"Backup script exploit"; content:"/cgi-bin/backup.sh"; http_uri; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

What change makes the IPS block the traffic?

options.text: Change the rule action from alert to drop (or reject)
Change the sid to a number below 1000000
Change the destination port from 8080 to any
Remove the http_uri modifier

explanation: An 'alert' action only logs; in inline mode a 'drop' or 'reject' action blocks matching traffic. Custom rules should use SIDs of 1,000,000 or above, so lowering it is wrong. Widening the port does not change the action. Removing http_uri changes where the content is matched, not whether traffic is blocked.

prompt: DLP rules inspect outbound uploads for sensitive data, but staff have been uploading password-protected ZIP files that the DLP engine cannot open. Which control closes this gap while allowing normal uploads?

options.text: Increase the DLP engine's maximum file size
A URL filtering rule that blocks the file-sharing category
Block uploads of encrypted or password-protected archives
Disable TLS inspection for file uploads

explanation: Blocking encrypted archives, which DLP cannot inspect, removes the bypass while other file types are still scanned and allowed. Blocking the file-sharing category stops legitimate uploads too and misses other destinations. A larger size limit does not help DLP read encrypted content. Disabling TLS inspection would make the gap wider.

prompt: A user signs in to a ZTNA-protected application from a compliant laptop. Twenty minutes later the EDR agent detects malware and marks the laptop as high risk, but the user's session stays active until the token expires eight hours later. Which Zero Trust principle is missing?

options.text: Microsegmentation of the application servers
Continuous verification of device risk during the session
Geofencing the user's sign-in location at each authentication
Longer password requirements at sign-in

explanation: Zero Trust requires trust to be re-evaluated continuously, so a change in device posture should end or restrict the session immediately rather than waiting for token expiry. Microsegmentation limits workload-to-workload traffic and does not react to device risk. Geofencing checks location, not device health. Password length affects only the initial sign-in.

prompt: Employees may use the company's tenant of a SaaS file-sharing service, but must be blocked in real time from uploading to personal accounts on the same service, which uses the same domains. Which CASB deployment mode enforces this?

options.text: API mode connected to the corporate tenant
Inline proxy mode enforcing tenant restrictions per session
A DNS filter blocking the service's domains
Log-based shadow IT discovery from firewall and proxy logs

explanation: Inline CASB sees each session as it happens, can tell the corporate tenant from personal instances, and blocks uploads to personal accounts in real time. API mode connects only to the corporate tenant and acts after data is stored, so it cannot see personal accounts. Log-based discovery reports usage but does not block. A DNS filter would block the corporate tenant too, since the domains are shared.

prompt: An attacker used an adversary-in-the-middle phishing page to capture a user's session cookie after the user completed MFA, then replayed the cookie from another country to access email. Which measures best reduce the risk of session token theft? (Choose two.)

options.text: Shorter session lifetimes with re-authentication for sensitive actions, and revoking sessions when risk is detected
Binding tokens to the device or client, and requiring phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2
Increasing password length to 16 characters
Disabling HTTPS to allow inspection of cookies
Switching from OIDC to SAML

explanation: Short-lived sessions, step-up re-authentication and revocation on risk limit how long a stolen session token stays useful, while device-bound tokens and FIDO2, which will not authenticate to a fake origin, stop the token being captured or replayed. Password length does not protect a token issued after login. Disabling HTTPS exposes tokens further. SAML sessions also rely on cookies, so switching protocol does not solve token theft.

prompt: A partner company's 300 engineers need access to a project portal. The partner runs its own identity provider and wants its staff to use their existing corporate accounts, with access ending automatically when they leave the partner. Which approach fits?

options.text: Create 300 local accounts in the portal and email the passwords
Share one portal account among all partner engineers
Grant the partner network access through a site-to-site VPN only
Federation with the partner's IdP, mapping groups to roles

explanation: Federation trusts the partner's IdP to authenticate its own users, so engineers use their existing accounts and lose access when the partner disables them. Local accounts must be created and removed by hand and often outlive the person. A shared account breaks accountability. A VPN provides network access but no user authentication to the portal.

prompt: An identity provider will issue access tokens for internal admin tools only when the endpoint presents a valid machine certificate from the corporate PKI and the EDR reports it as healthy. If EDR later reports compromise, the endpoint's sessions are revoked. Which IAM concept is this design applying?

options.text: Role-based access control based on job function
Just-in-time account provisioning at first login
Endpoint trust as an access condition
Single sign-on federation across services

explanation: The design makes the endpoint's verified identity and health a condition for issuing and keeping tokens, which is endpoint trust. RBAC assigns permissions by role but does not consider device state. JIT provisioning creates accounts at first login. SSO federation lets users sign in once across services, but says nothing about the endpoint's health.

prompt: A café wants its public Wi-Fi to stay open, with no password to share, but it wants each customer's traffic encrypted over the air so other customers cannot sniff it. Which option meets this?

options.text: Wi-Fi Enhanced Open (OWE)
WPA2-Personal with the password printed on the menu
An open SSID with a captive portal
WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X

explanation: Enhanced Open uses Opportunistic Wireless Encryption to give each client its own encryption keys without any password. A shared WPA2 password printed publicly lets anyone who knows it decrypt others' traffic once they capture the handshake. A captive portal on an open SSID leaves traffic unencrypted. 802.1X requires credentials for every user, which does not suit a public café.

prompt: An organisation uses WPA2-Enterprise with PEAP-MSCHAPv2. A penetration tester set up an evil twin AP with its own RADIUS server and captured MSCHAPv2 challenge-responses from laptops whose supplicants accepted any server certificate. What fixes the weakness?

options.text: Hide the corporate SSID so the evil twin cannot copy it
Switch the SSID to WPA2-Personal
Enforce server certificate validation, or use EAP-TLS
Enable MAC address filtering on the APs

explanation: If supplicants validate the RADIUS server's certificate against a trusted CA and expected name, they will not send credentials to an impostor; EAP-TLS removes passwords altogether. Hiding the SSID does not stop an evil twin. WPA2-Personal replaces individual credentials with a shared key and is weaker. MAC filtering does not protect clients from a fake AP.

prompt: A critical firmware patch must be rolled out to 400 access switches. What is the best approach to deploy it and verify success?

options.text: Install it on all 400 switches at once during one night
Pilot first, verify version and health, then roll out in waves
Install it everywhere, then check only that each switch answers ping
Install it only on switches that report problems

explanation: A staged rollout limits the impact of a bad patch, and verifying the running version and health after each wave confirms success before continuing. Patching everything at once risks a campus-wide outage. Patching only switches with problems leaves the others vulnerable. Ping proves reachability, not that the right version is running or that services work.

prompt: A scan from outside shows that the internet edge router announces its model, software version and interface names to anyone connected to its ISP-facing port. Which hardening step addresses this?

options.text: Change the router's hostname
Enable SNMPv3 on the ISP-facing interface
Disable CDP and LLDP on external-facing interfaces
Enable a login banner on the router

explanation: Discovery protocols such as CDP and LLDP advertise device details to neighbours, so they should be disabled on untrusted interfaces. SNMPv3 is a management protocol and does not stop discovery advertisements. A new hostname hides one detail but not the model or version. A banner does not change what the router advertises.

prompt: Network devices authenticate administrators through TACACS+. During a TACACS+ outage nobody could log in, so the team is adding a local account. How should local authentication be configured?

options.text: Use the local account first and TACACS+ only if the local login fails
Remove TACACS+ and use local accounts on each device instead
Create the same local admin password on every device and share it with all engineers
TACACS+ first, vaulted local fallback only if servers are unreachable

explanation: Using TACACS+ first with local fallback only when the servers cannot be reached keeps central authentication and accounting, and a vaulted, monitored break-glass account limits misuse. Using local first bypasses central AAA for normal logins. A shared password on all devices is risky and gives no accountability. Removing TACACS+ loses central control and per-command accounting.

prompt: A company is inviting three vendors to bid on a WAN redesign and must give them current network diagrams, IP plans and firewall designs. Which agreement should be in place before these documents are shared?

options.text: A non-disclosure agreement with each vendor
A master service agreement with each vendor
An interconnection security agreement
A service-level agreement

explanation: An NDA legally obliges each vendor to keep the shared design information confidential, which is needed before an award decision. An MSA sets commercial terms for an ongoing relationship and is premature for bidders. An ISA covers the technical security of connecting two organisations' systems. An SLA defines service levels for a delivered service.

prompt: Virtual firewall appliances in the cloud autoscale from 2 to 10 instances at peak. The company bought perpetual bring-your-own licences for only 4 instances, so scaled-out instances fail to pass traffic. Which licensing approach best fits the burst pattern?

options.text: BYOL for the baseline plus pay-as-you-go for burst instances
Disable autoscaling and cap the group at 4 instances
Buy 10 perpetual licences and leave 6 idle most of the time
Run the burst instances without licences, since they are short-lived

explanation: A hybrid model, with owned licences for steady capacity and per-hour pay-as-you-go licences for burst instances, matches cost to use while keeping every instance licensed. Buying 10 perpetual licences pays for capacity that sits idle. Capping at 4 sacrifices peak capacity. Running unlicensed instances breaks the licensing agreement and they will not pass traffic anyway.

prompt: Opening a new retail branch currently takes eight weeks because router and firewall appliances must be ordered, staged and shipped. The business wants branches online within days and wants store managers to request standard network services without filing tickets. Which approach best meets this?

options.text: Keep a larger stock of pre-staged physical appliances in the warehouse
Hire more engineers to stage and ship appliances faster
Lease dark fiber to every new branch
Self-service, automatically provisioned virtual network functions

explanation: Network function virtualisation runs routing and firewall functions as software, and a self-service catalogue with automated provisioning delivers approved designs in days, improving time to market. Extra stock and more engineers shorten some steps but keep the manual hardware process. Dark fiber is slow to build and does nothing for service provisioning.

prompt: An external auditor must confirm that every firewall rule change in the past year was authorised. Which evidence best supports this audit?

options.text: Device change logs reconciled against approved change tickets
A current export of the firewall rule base with hit counts
Interviews with the firewall administrators and their managers
The firewall vendor's product datasheet

explanation: Auditing authorisation means comparing what actually changed, from device change logs, with what was approved in change records, and following up on gaps. A current rule export shows the end state, not who changed what or whether it was approved. Interviews are not objective evidence. A datasheet describes product features, not the company's changes.

prompt: A monitoring system pings a cloud web server every minute and reports it down, yet customers are using the site without problems. The server's security group allows only TCP 443 inbound. What should be changed?

options.text: Allow ICMP from anywhere on the security group
Use a TCP or HTTPS check on port 443 instead
Increase the ping timeout to 10 seconds
Move the monitoring system into the same subnet as the server

explanation: The security group drops ICMP, so ping fails while HTTPS works; a TCP or HTTPS check tests the path and service users actually rely on. Opening ICMP to the world widens exposure just to satisfy the monitor. A longer timeout cannot help when ICMP is dropped. Moving the monitor into the subnet still meets the same rule and no longer tests external reachability.

prompt: The NOC polls interface status on core routers every five minutes, so link failures sometimes go unnoticed for minutes. It wants immediate notification when a link goes down, without polling every few seconds. What should be configured?

options.text: SNMP traps or informs for link-down events
SNMP polling every 5 seconds
Daily interface reports from the NMS
NetFlow export from the routers

explanation: SNMP traps and informs are sent by the device as soon as an event such as link-down happens, so the NMS learns of it at once; informs are acknowledged and resent if lost. Polling every 5 seconds puts heavy load on devices and the NMS. Daily reports are far too slow. NetFlow describes traffic flows, not interface state changes.

prompt: While investigating an incident, analysts cannot line up events from firewalls, switches and cloud services in the central logging platform. Some devices log in local time, others drift by several minutes, and cloud logs use UTC. What should be fixed first?

options.text: Increase log retention to two years
Move all logs into a single data lake with one schema
Sync clocks to common NTP and log in UTC
Raise the logging level to debug on all devices

explanation: Correlation depends on accurate, consistent timestamps, so all sources need synchronised clocks and a common time format such as UTC. Longer retention keeps more data but leaves it misaligned. Moving logs into a data lake does not correct timestamps. Debug logging adds noise without fixing time alignment.

prompt: The network team adds VLANs to access switches several times a week with a tested automation template that has never caused an incident. Each change currently waits a week for the change advisory board. How should change management handle this?

options.text: Treat each VLAN addition as an emergency change to skip the CAB
Stop recording the VLAN changes to save time
Make it a pre-approved standard change, still logged
Require the CAB to meet daily

explanation: Low-risk, repeatable changes with a proven procedure can be pre-approved as standard changes, which are still recorded but do not need CAB review each time. Using the emergency process for routine work misuses it. Not recording changes breaks audit and troubleshooting. Daily CAB meetings add overhead to a change that is already proven safe.

prompt:
An engineer runs the same configuration playbook against 12 switches twice in a row. The second run ends with:

PLAY RECAP
sw01 : ok=14 changed=0 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=1
... (same for sw02 to sw12)

What does this output indicate?

options.text: The playbook failed to connect to the switches
The switches already match the desired state, so nothing changed
The second run reverted the changes made by the first run
The playbook ran in check mode on the first run

explanation: With changed=0, failed=0 and unreachable=0, every task found the device already in the declared state, which is the expected result of idempotent desired-state automation on a second run. Connection failures would show as unreachable. A revert would show changes. The recap does not show check mode, and the first run is not described here.

prompt: A script that updates firewall objects through a cloud provider's REST API starts failing partway through a large batch with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses that include a Retry-After header. What should the script do?

options.text: Retry each failed request immediately in a tight loop
Generate a new API key for every request
Switch from HTTPS to HTTP to reduce per-request overhead
Honour Retry-After with exponential backoff and jitter

explanation: HTTP 429 means the client exceeded a rate limit; waiting as instructed by Retry-After and backing off exponentially lets the batch complete without overloading the API. Immediate retries make throttling worse. Dropping TLS is insecure and does not change rate limits. New keys for each request may break policy and still count against account limits.

prompt: One user reports that a CRM application freezes 'every so often', and no one else has complained. Monitoring shows nothing unusual. Before forming a theory, what should the engineer try to do?

options.text: Close the ticket because no other users are affected by it
Replace the user's laptop immediately
Restart the CRM servers during business hours
Reproduce it with the user on the same device and network

explanation: Duplicating the problem when possible, ideally with the user on the same device and location, gives concrete symptoms, times and conditions to investigate. Replacing the laptop is a fix without a theory. Restarting servers affects every user without evidence. A single affected user is still a valid problem to investigate.

prompt: Users can reach every application except one, which returns 'HTTP 503 Service Unavailable' with the application's own branded error page. Which troubleshooting approach is most efficient?

options.text: Top-to-bottom, starting at the application and its backends
Replace the core switches one by one
Start at layer 1 and check every cable between users and the data centre
Check for duplex mismatches on all user switch ports

explanation: A branded 503 page shows that the network path and the web front end are working, so starting at the application layer and working down is quickest, for example checking backend health and pool membership. Starting at layer 1 ignores clear evidence that lower layers work. Replacing core switches is unjustified. Duplex problems would affect many applications, not one.

prompt: An engineer suspects a Linux server is sending DNS queries to an unexpected resolver. She wants to watch DNS traffic on eth0 in real time with IP addresses and port numbers shown numerically, not resolved. Which command should she use?

options.text: tcpdump -i eth0 port 80
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 53
netstat -rn
dig @127.0.0.1 example.com

explanation: tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 53 captures DNS traffic on that interface and -nn prevents name and port resolution, so the destination resolver IP is shown directly. Port 80 captures HTTP, not DNS. dig sends a query to the resolver you name, which does not show what the server normally uses. netstat -rn shows the routing table.

prompt: A web application sits behind a load balancer. An engineer wants to send an HTTPS request for app.example.com straight to one backend server at 10.0.5.21, with correct SNI and certificate checking, and see the full request and response headers. Which command should be used?

options.text: nslookup app.example.com 10.0.5.21
curl -v --resolve app.example.com:443:10.0.5.21 https://app.example.com/

explanation: --resolve maps app.example.com to the backend IP for this request only, so curl sends the right SNI and Host header and checks the certificate against the hostname, while -v shows the headers. ping tests only ICMP reachability. nslookup would query the backend as if it were a DNS server. curl -I over plain HTTP to the IP sends no SNI and skips TLS entirely.

prompt: On a Windows server, an unknown program keeps an outbound connection open to an external IP on TCP 4444. The engineer needs to find which process owns the connection. Which command shows the owning process ID for each connection?

options.text: ipconfig /all
netstat -ano
route print
arp -a

explanation: netstat -ano lists all connections and listening ports numerically with the owning process ID, which can then be matched to a program in Task Manager or with tasklist. ipconfig /all shows interface configuration. route print shows the routing table. arp -a shows IP-to-MAC mappings on the local network.

prompt: An on-site Wi-Fi survey heat map of a warehouse shows -55 to -65 dBm across most aisles, but a region of high racking at the north end shows -78 to -84 dBm, where handheld scanners disconnect. Noise is -92 dBm throughout. What does the heat map indicate?

options.text: Co-channel interference between the APs in the north end
Excessive noise from non-Wi-Fi sources at the north end
A rogue AP operating at the north end
A coverage gap caused by racking; add or move an AP

explanation: Signal of -78 to -84 dBm with a normal noise floor shows weak coverage, a gap caused by dense racking, which is fixed by adding or moving APs or using directional antennas. Co-channel interference appears as high channel utilisation with strong signal from several APs, not weak signal. A rogue AP would appear as an extra transmitter. The noise floor is the same everywhere, so noise is not the cause.

prompt:
An automation job calling a network controller API through Postman suddenly fails. The response is:

Status: 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="The access token expired"

What should be done?

options.text: Add the job's account to an administrator group, since this is an authorisation failure
Retry the request with exponential backoff, since the API is rate limiting
Get a new access token and resend the request
Change the request method from GET to POST

explanation: The 401 with invalid_token and 'access token expired' means the bearer token is no longer valid, so the client must get a new one and retry. A permissions problem would normally return 403 Forbidden for a valid token. Rate limiting returns 429. Changing the method does not fix an expired token.

prompt:
A SIEM correlation alert summarises the last hour of identity provider logs:

source_ip: 203.0.113.77
failed_logins: 412
distinct_usernames: 409
password_hash_matches: 1 distinct password used
successful_logins: 3 (j.ortiz, m.chen, svc-print)

Which attack is this, and what should be done first?

options.text: Credential stuffing from breached username and password pairs; enforce breached-password screening only
A brute-force attack on a single account; lock that account
Password spraying; block the source, reset the three accounts, revoke sessions, enforce MFA
A denial-of-service attack on the identity provider; add capacity

explanation: One source trying a single password against hundreds of accounts is password spraying, and three accounts used that password; they must be reset with sessions revoked, the source blocked, and MFA enforced. Credential stuffing uses many different username and password pairs. Brute force targets one account with many passwords. About 400 attempts in an hour is not a volume that denies service.

prompt:
After an administrator cloned several VMs from a template that had a static MAC address, the access switch logs show:

%SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF: Host 0050.56aa.1234 in vlan 40 is flapping between port Gi1/0/5 and port Gi1/0/9

Users of the cloned VMs report intermittent connectivity. What is the cause?

options.text: Duplicate MAC addresses on the cloned VMs cause MAC flapping
A spanning tree loop between ports Gi1/0/5 and Gi1/0/9
DHCP scope exhaustion in VLAN 40
An IPv6 router advertisement from one of the VMs

explanation: Clones that share a static MAC make the switch move that MAC between the ports where the VMs live, so frames go to the wrong VM and connectivity is intermittent; each VM needs a unique MAC. A loop would produce flapping of many MACs and broadcast storms, not one host's address. Scope exhaustion stops address assignment rather than causing MAC flapping. Router advertisements affect default routes, not MAC learning.

prompt: On Monday morning, new visitors on the guest Wi-Fi cannot get IP addresses, while people already connected keep working. The DHCP server log shows 'DHCPDISCOVER from 3c:22:fb:1a:09:7e via 10.80.0.1: network 10.80.0.0/24: no free leases'. The scope uses an 8-day lease time. What is the best fix?

options.text: Shorten the guest lease time and, if needed, enlarge the subnet
Restart the DHCP server to clear the log and stale leases
Assign static IP addresses to guest devices on arrival
Move the DHCP relay address to a different interface on the guest router

explanation: The /24 pool is exhausted because transient guest devices hold leases for 8 days; short leases free addresses quickly, and a larger subnet adds headroom. A restart does not release active leases. Static addresses cannot be managed for unknown guest devices. The relay works, as the server received the discover, so moving it does nothing.

prompt: IPv4 file transfers across a new tunnel work, but IPv6 transfers to the same servers stall after the TCP handshake. The edge firewall's IPv6 policy blocks all ICMPv6 apart from echo. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Blocked ICMPv6 Packet Too Big breaks path MTU discovery
The IPv6 default route is missing on the servers
DNS is returning the wrong AAAA records
IPv6 routers fragment packets in transit, and the firewall drops the fragments

explanation: IPv6 routers never fragment; senders rely on ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages to discover the path MTU, so blocking them makes large packets disappear after the handshake. RFC 4890 says these messages must be allowed. It is the hosts, not routers, that fragment IPv6. A missing default route or wrong AAAA record would stop the handshake from completing.

prompt: Every weekday from 10:00 to 12:00, users at a regional office see slow applications. Flow data shows a nightly backup job, which now overruns into the morning, using 95% of the 200 Mbps WAN link. What is the best fix?

options.text: Enable jumbo frames on the WAN link to move data more efficiently
Deprioritise or rate-limit the backups and finish them off-hours
Replace the office switches
Increase DNS cache sizes on user laptops

explanation: The link is overutilised by bulk backup traffic, so limiting or deprioritising it and ensuring it finishes outside business hours restores performance for users. Jumbo frames do not reduce the volume and are rarely supported across WANs. The office switches are not the bottleneck. DNS caching has nothing to do with link saturation.

prompt: APs in a clinic were set to maximum transmit power (about 23 dBm), while the handheld devices transmit at about 14 dBm. Devices at the edge of each cell show full signal bars but have high retry rates and drop frequently. What is the problem, and what is the fix?

options.text: Channel width too narrow; increase it to 80 MHz for more throughput
Band steering misconfiguration; disable 5 GHz
A captive portal timeout; extend the session time
Asymmetric link; lower AP power to match the clients

explanation: With the AP much louder than the clients, clients see a strong signal and stay associated even where their own weaker transmissions are not heard well by the AP, which causes retries and drops; matching AP power to the client capability fixes the imbalance. Wider channels make reception harder, not easier. Band steering problems affect which band clients join. Captive portal timeouts do not cause retries.

prompt: Users on Wi-Fi calls are dropped whenever they walk from building A to building B. Each building's WLAN controller places the SSID on a different VLAN and subnet, and clients receive a new IP address after roaming. What should be fixed?

options.text: Increase AP transmit power at both building entrances and walkways
Disable 802.11r on the SSID
Layer 3 roaming with mobility tunnelling, or a shared VLAN
Shorten the DHCP lease time in both buildings

explanation: Getting a new IP address on roaming breaks active sessions; controller mobility groups that tunnel the client back to its anchor, or a shared VLAN, let clients keep their address across buildings. More transmit power does not keep the IP address. Disabling 802.11r slows roaming further. Shorter leases do not stop the subnet change.

prompt: A new internal CA template was copied from a legacy system. Since then, browsers reject newly issued intranet certificates even though the chain and names are correct. The certificate details show 'Signature algorithm: sha1WithRSAEncryption'. What is the problem?

options.text: The certificates use RSA, which browsers no longer support
The certificates' SAN field is too long
The root CA has been revoked
SHA-1 signatures are rejected; reissue with SHA-256

explanation: Modern browsers and TLS libraries reject certificates signed with SHA-1 because of collision attacks, so the template must use SHA-256 or stronger and the certificates must be reissued. RSA keys are still widely supported. A revoked root would cause revocation errors, and nothing shows that here. SAN length is not the issue, and the names are correct.

prompt:
An application in a new container image fails to call an internal API, while the same call works from engineers' laptops. From inside the container:

$ openssl s_client -connect api.corp.example:443 -servername api.corp.example
...
Certificate chain
 0 s:CN = api.corp.example
   i:CN = Corp Issuing CA
 1 s:CN = Corp Issuing CA
   i:CN = Corp Root CA
 2 s:CN = Corp Root CA
   i:CN = Corp Root CA
verify error:num=19:self-signed certificate in certificate chain

What is the cause?

options.text: The server is missing its intermediate certificate
The container's trust store lacks the internal Corp Root CA
The API certificate has expired
The certificate's name does not match api.corp.example

explanation: The server sends the full chain up to Corp Root CA, but the container does not trust that self-signed root, so verification fails; adding the internal root to the image's trust store fixes it, while laptops already trust it. The intermediate is present in the chain. An expired certificate would report an expiry error. The leaf CN matches the requested name.

prompt:
Monitoring reports that HTTPS to the partner portal is failing. An engineer checks the certificate:

$ echo | openssl s_client -connect portal.example.com:443 -servername portal.example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
notBefore=Aug 25 00:00:00 2026 GMT
notAfter=Nov 22 23:59:59 2026 GMT

Today is 23 November 2026. What should be done, and how can this be prevented?

options.text: Renew the certificate and automate renewal with ACME and alerts
Change the server's clock back by two days so it is valid again
Disable certificate validation on the clients
Add the certificate to a CRL

explanation: The certificate expired the day before, so it must be renewed and deployed; automated renewal with ACME and expiry monitoring prevent a repeat with short-lived certificates. Changing the server clock does not change the clients' view of validity and breaks other services. Disabling validation removes TLS protection. A CRL is for revoking certificates, not renewing them.
